overview.title: 📖 Overview: Closing the Shabbatot Debate, Opening Uncertainty
overview.subtitle: Keritot 17a–17b
overview.hebrewSource: יֵשׁ אֵם לַמָּסוֹרֶת... יֵשׁ אֵם לַמִּקְרָא
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf completes the intricate analysis of Rabbi Akiva's Shabbat dilemma, testing the competing reconstructions of Rava and Rav Ḥisda against small but decisive linguistic details in the mishna's wording — singular or plural 'menstruating woman,' singular or plural 'minor girls.' A parallel baraita even records a wholly different version of Rabbi Akiva's question, framed around repeated intercourse with a menstruating wife rather than Shabbat labor. The chapter then closes, and a new mishna opens the Torah's treatment of the provisional guilt offering (asham talui) — brought whenever genuine uncertainty exists about whether a sin was committed at all. The Gemara spends the rest of the daf on a foundational dispute between Rav Asi and Ḥiyya bar Rav over whether a single doubtful piece of fat, or only a doubt between two pieces, triggers this offering — a dispute rooted in how a single Hebrew word in the Torah is spelled versus how it is read aloud.

slides.title: 🧵 One Body or Many? Testing the Shabbatot Theories
slides.subtitle: The Gemara hunts for proof in a single word's grammatical number

nodes.content: 🔍 Rav Ḥisda's theory requires Rabbi Eliezer's menstrual-woman proof to use the SINGULAR ('menstruating woman') — since his dilemma was about intervening days, not separate bodies
🔍 Rava's theory requires the PLURAL ('menstruating women') — since his dilemma was about whether Shabbatot count as separate bodies
📜 Textual tradition is split: Shmuel and Rav Adda bar Ahava transmit the singular; Rav Natan bar Oshaya transmits the plural — the manuscript evidence itself doesn't settle it
🧩 Rava must still explain the singular version: he posits a case of repeated intercourse with immersions IN BETWEEN, so the immersions function like 'intervening days' even under his own theory

✅ The 'minor girls' proof, by contrast, appears in the plural regardless — fitting Rava's theory naturally (separate girls = separate bodies), while Rav Ḥisda must read it merely as 'minor girls in general,' not one man with several

callout.label: Net result:
callout.text: Neither theory is fully disproven — each requires its own careful reading of the mishna's grammatical choices.

slides.title: 🔄 A Different Question Entirely?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: Rabbi Akiva never asked about Shabbat at all

lines.speaker: R' Shimon b. Elazar
lines.text: That's not what Rabbi Akiva asked Rabbi Eliezer! He really asked: if one unwittingly has relations with his menstruating wife, then again, in one lapse of awareness — one offering or many?

lines.speaker: R' Eliezer
lines.text: Liable for each! A fortiori from SHABBAT: it has only ONE warning (he is warned about it, but it isn't warned about him), yet each labor is separately liable. A menstruating woman has TWO mutual warnings — surely each act is liable too!

lines.speaker: R' Akiva
lines.text: Not comparable — Shabbat has MANY categories of labor generating multiple sin offerings; a menstruating woman has only ONE type of forbidden act.

lines.speaker: R' Eliezer
lines.text: Then minor girls prove it — no multiplicity of acts there either, yet each girl is separately liable!

lines.speaker: R' Akiva
lines.text: Not comparable — minors are separate BODIES. A repeatedly-violated single wife is not.

lines.speaker: R' Eliezer
lines.text: Then bestiality proves it — no separate bodies there, yet still liable per act!

lines.speaker: R' Akiva
lines.text: I treat the animal case as just as uncertain as the menstruating-wife case itself.

callout.label: Striking reversal:
callout.text: In this version, the ENTIRE debate about Shabbat is repurposed — the exact same a fortiori chain, but now proving something about repeated forbidden intercourse instead.

slides.title: ❓ New Mishna: The Provisional Guilt Offering
slides.subtitle: Chapter three opens: what triggers an asham talui (offering for uncertain sin)?
rows: Uncertain whether he ate forbidden fat at all
Definitely ate, but uncertain if the piece met the minimum measure
Permitted and forbidden fat both present; ate one, doesn't know which
Wife and sister both present; had relations with one, doesn't know which
Confused Shabbat and a weekday; performed labor on one, doesn't know which

callout.label: Parallel structure to sin offerings:
callout.text: Just as eating two pieces of forbidden fat in one lapse yields one sin offering (but eating fat, blood, piggul, and notar together yields separate offerings for each), the same multiplication rules govern the provisional guilt offering for uncertain violations.

slides.title: 📖 Written or Read? Mesorah vs. Mikra
slides.subtitle: Does the provisional guilt offering require doubt about ONE item or between TWO?

lines.speaker: Verse
lines.text: Leviticus 4:22 is spelled מִצְוַת (mitzvat, singular) but traditionally READ as מִצְווֹת (mitzvot, plural).

lines.speaker: Rav Asi
lines.text: The written spelling governs (יֵשׁ אֵם לַמָּסוֹרֶת) — singular. So even doubt about a SINGLE piece (is it forbidden fat or permitted fat?) triggers the offering.

lines.speaker: Ḥiyya bar Rav
lines.text: The spoken reading governs (יֵשׁ אֵם לַמִּקְרָא) — plural. So the offering requires doubt between TWO distinct pieces, one definitely forbidden and one definitely permitted.

lines.speaker: Rav's parallel ruling
lines.text: Confirms Ḥiyya's approach: two pieces before him, ate one, unknown which → liable. But ONE piece of inherently uncertain status (perhaps forbidden, perhaps not) → exempt.

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: This single grammatical question determines the entire boundary of when 'uncertainty' is serious enough to require an offering at all.

slides.title: 🧪 Two Theories for Rav's Ruling — And Where They Diverge
slides.subtitle: Why does a single doubtful piece differ from a doubt between two known pieces?

boxes.title: Rava's theory: the verse requires 'two'
items: Grounded purely in reading מִצְווֹת as plural
A single piece never qualifies, no matter what
Challenged by Rabbi Eliezer's koy case (single uncertain animal) — resolved as Rabbi Eliezer following the OTHER reading (mesorah, singular)

boxes.title: Rabbi Zeira's theory: the doubt must be resolvable
items: Two known pieces let an expert LATER examine the leftover piece and determine what was eaten
A single ambiguous piece can never be resolved this way — nothing remains to test

Diverges from Rava's theory in an edge case: one full olive-bulk piece plus a mere half-olive-bulk piece — Rava exempts (not 'two' qualifying pieces), Rabbi Zeira still obligates (the remainder can still be examined)

callout.label: Rabbi Eliezer's koy exception:
callout.text: Both theories must explain why Rabbi Eliezer obligates an offering even for a single-item doubt (the mixed-species koy) — resolved as his own minority position, following the written mesorah over the two-item requirement.

summary.principle: Establishing exactly when uncertainty is severe enough to require a provisional guilt offering — like establishing when repeated acts multiply liability — depends on precise textual and conceptual distinctions, down to how a single word is spelled versus how it is traditionally read aloud.

flowSteps.content: 🧵 Grammatical number in the mishna's wording is tested to arbitrate between two theories of Rabbi Akiva's Shabbat dilemma
🔄 A competing baraita reframes the entire debate around repeated forbidden intercourse instead of Shabbat
❓ A new mishna catalogs five scenarios of genuine uncertainty that trigger a provisional guilt offering

columns.content: 📖 Rav Asi and Ḥiyya bar Rav dispute whether the Torah's spelling or its reading governs the offering's scope
🧪 Rava and Rabbi Zeira propose different rationales for Rav's ruling, diverging in edge cases

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: even the smallest textual details — a word's spelling, its grammatical number — can determine the entire scope of a halakha

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's alternate account, what did Rabbi Akiva actually ask Rabbi Eliezer, instead of the Shabbat question found in the primary version of the mishna?
o: Whether an animal's dangling limb transmits impurity
Whether repeated unwitting intercourse with one's menstruating wife, in a single lapse of awareness, generates one sin offering or many
Whether five offerings slaughtered outside the Temple require one or five sin offerings
Whether a convert's offering must include an animal
quiz.e: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reports a different version of Rabbi Akiva's question, about repeated intercourse with a menstruating wife, using an inverted a fortiori chain built from Shabbat instead of resolved through it.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, which of the following situations obligates a person to bring a provisional guilt offering (asham talui)?
o: He definitely ate a forbidden food and knows exactly what it was
He had relations with either his wife or his sister (both present) but does not know with which one
He performed no labor at all on Shabbat
He is certain he did not sin
quiz.e: The mishna lists genuine uncertainty as the trigger for a provisional guilt offering — including cases like an ambiguous partner, ambiguous food, or ambiguous day, where the person cannot determine which of two real possibilities occurred.

quiz.q: What is the basis of the dispute between Rav Asi and Ḥiyya bar Rav over whether a provisional guilt offering requires uncertainty about one item or two?
o: A disagreement about the price of offerings
Whether the Torah's authoritative form is its written spelling (mesorah) or its traditional pronunciation (mikra) of the word for 'commandments'
A dispute about which Temple gate to use
Whether the offering must be an animal or a bird
quiz.e: Rav Asi holds the written spelling (singular 'mitzvat') is authoritative, permitting a single-item doubt to trigger the offering; Ḥiyya bar Rav holds the spoken reading (plural 'mitzvot') is authoritative, requiring doubt between two items.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Zeira's explanation of Rav's ruling, why does a doubt involving two distinct pieces of fat (one forbidden, one permitted) trigger a provisional guilt offering, while a single piece of inherently uncertain status does not?
o: Because two pieces are always heavier than one
Because with two known pieces, an expert can later examine the leftover piece to resolve what was actually eaten, while a single ambiguous piece can never be resolved this way
Because Rav prohibited eating two pieces at once
Because two pieces always weigh more than an olive-bulk
quiz.e: Rabbi Zeira's rationale is that the doubt must be resolvable — with two distinct pieces, examining the leftover piece can clarify which was forbidden, but a single ambiguous piece offers no such possibility for resolution.

quiz.q: How do both Rava's and Rabbi Zeira's theories account for Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that one is obligated in a provisional guilt offering for eating the fat of a koy (an animal of uncertain single-item status)?
o: They both reject Rabbi Eliezer's ruling as unreliable

Both explain that Rabbi Eliezer follows the alternative principle — that the written form (singular) is authoritative, or that resolvability is not required — making his ruling a recognized minority position
They claim the koy is actually two animals
They say the koy case has nothing to do with fat at all
quiz.e: Both theories must account for Rabbi Eliezer's single-item koy ruling by attributing it to his adoption of the alternative principle (mesorah over mikra, or no need for resolvability), distinguishing his view from Rav's general ruling.
